extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant recipients (PIs and grant administrative staff) preparing interim or final RPPR Project Outcomes summaries
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing the Section I Project Outcomes summary in an interim or final NIH Research Performance Progress Report (RPPR). The summary should communicate cumulative outcomes/findings for public reporting (NIH RePORTER) in plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Project Outcome summaries should not exceed half a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the summary very brief — essentially a short (≤ half page) plain-language summary suitable for public display. See examples on the page for typical length and level of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and language (public-friendly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is written for the general public in clear, concise, and comprehensible language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid technical jargon; explain concepts in plain English so non-experts can understand. Use concise sentences and focus on the main findings and their implications rather than methodological minutiae. The provided examples show how to translate technical results into accessible statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for public dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: Is suitable for dissemination to the general public, as the information may be available electronically (made public via NIH RePORTER).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the summary will be posted online and read by broad audiences; emphasize clarity, context, and relevance. Do not include information that would be inappropriate for public release.

rubrics_metrics.name: No proprietary, confidential, or trade-secret information
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not include proprietary, confidential information or trade secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude unpublished proprietary details, confidential business information, or trade secrets. If aspects of the work are sensitive, describe outcomes at a high level without revealing protected information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content: cumulative outcomes/findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Project Outcomes provide information regarding the cumulative outcomes or findings of the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the project's overall results to date (cumulative findings), key conclusions, and why they matter. Examples show stating the study question, follow-up duration or sample context, main results (including magnitude and statistical relevance when important), notable subgroup findings, and potential implications for health or future research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase III clinical trials — include valid analyses by sex and race/ethnicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients conducting an NIH-defined Phase III Clinical Trial must include results of valid analyses by sex and race and/or ethnicity in the Project Outcome Summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For NIH-defined Phase III trials, report results broken down by sex and race/ethnicity when valid analyses are possible. See the NIH 'Valid Analysis for NIH-defined Phase III Clinical Trials' guidance for details on what constitutes valid analyses and how to report them. The VITAL example on the page illustrates inclusion of subgroup/race-specific findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include identifying metadata (as exemplified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include brief identifying metadata such as Project title, Contact PI, and Organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the page presents examples that show Project, Contact PI, and Organization at the top of the summary, follow your RPPR form/field structure for required metadata. Use these fields to help the public identify the study and responsible investigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model structure/content illustrated by examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples demonstrate desirable components and tone for a Project Outcomes summary (brief background/context, concise description of main findings, subgroup differences, and implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the examples as models: give a one-sentence study context (what was tested and population), brief description of follow-up/sample size if relevant, state main results plainly (percent changes, direction of effect, statistical significance if informative), note important subgroup findings or heterogeneity, and conclude with high-level implications or next steps. Keep it concise and public-facing.
